title: Dagbon: The Kingdom of the Drum Historians

pages.text: It is evening in front of the palace at Yendi. A drummer steps forward with a drum shaped like an hourglass, held under his arm. As he squeezes its strings, the drum’s voice rises and falls like a person speaking. He begins to chant. He names a king who ruled five hundred years ago, then that king’s son, then the next, and on through the night. He holds no book. In Dagbon, the drummers are the historians. They are called lunsi, and what they carry in memory is the story of one of the oldest kingdoms in Ghana.

As he squeezes its strings, the drum’s voice rises and falls like a person speaking.
He begins to chant.
He names a king who ruled five hundred years ago, then that king’s son, then the next, and on through the night.
He holds no book.
In Dagbon, the drummers are the historians.
They are called lunsi, and what they carry in memory is the story of one of the oldest kingdoms in Ghana.
pages.alt: A drummer in a smock playing an hourglass-shaped drum under his arm before a round palace building at dusk.

pages.text: The lunsi begin with a hunter. Tradition says that long ago a brave man called Tohazie, the red hunter, came from the east. His grandson, Naa Gbewaa, settled at Pusiga, near Bawku in the far north-east of Ghana, and ruled there. After Gbewaa died, his children quarrelled and went different ways. One son founded Mamprugu, with its king, the Nayiri, at Nalerigu. Another, Sitobu, founded Dagbon. A third founded Nanung, around Bimbilla. To this day, the three kingdoms call one another brothers, and Mamprugu is honoured as the eldest.

Tradition says that long ago a brave man called Tohazie, the red hunter, came from the east.
His grandson, Naa Gbewaa, settled at Pusiga, near Bawku in the far north-east of Ghana, and ruled there.
After Gbewaa died, his children quarrelled and went different ways.
One son founded Mamprugu, with its king, the Nayiri, at Nalerigu.
Another, Sitobu, founded Dagbon.
A third founded Nanung, around Bimbilla.
To this day, the three kingdoms call one another brothers, and Mamprugu is honoured as the eldest.
pages.alt: A map of northern Ghana marking Pusiga, Nalerigu, Yendi, and Bimbilla, joined by arrows from Pusiga.

pages.text: Sitobu’s son, Naa Nyagse, made Dagbon large. Riding with horsemen, he brought town after town under his rule, in about the 1400s, and placed his sons and relatives over them as chiefs. The king took the title Ya-Na. The first capital stood in the west of the kingdom. In the 1600s, after wars with the neighbouring kingdom of Gonja, the capital was moved east to the place now called Yendi. In the north, a chief does not sit on a stool. He sits on the skins of animals, and so a new chief is said to be enskinned.

pages.alt: Horsemen in flowing robes riding across open grassland towards a town of round houses.

pages.text: Around 1700, a king named Naa Zanjina came to the skin. He is remembered as the Ya-Na who welcomed Islam, invited Muslim teachers and traders, and encouraged weaving and trade. Dagbon lay on the road between the forest and the markets of Hausaland, far to the north-east. Kola nuts, salt, cloth, and cattle passed through its towns. Later in the 1700s, Asante became the stronger power, and for many years Dagbon had to send tribute to Kumasi. Yet the kingdom kept its own king, its own laws, and its own drummers.

pages.text: You can see Dagbon’s history in its festivals. At Damba, chiefs in great smocks ride decorated horses, and the people dance to the lunsi. At the Fire Festival, crowds carry burning torches of grass through the night. You can wear that history too. The smock, sewn from strips of hand-woven cotton, is now national dress, worn across Ghana. Dagbon has known trouble as well, including a long and painful dispute over who should be king. In 2019, with the help of other chiefs, a new Ya-Na was enskinned in peace.

pages.text: Think again about the drummer at Yendi. A boy born into a family of lunsi starts to learn as a small child. He must remember hundreds of names, praises, and stories exactly, and he will teach them to the children after him. In this way, a history has travelled across five centuries without paper. Written records are not the only records. When an old drummer or storyteller dies with his knowledge unrecorded, a library is lost. Ghana needs its books, and it needs people who will listen, learn, and write down what the elders know.

activities.question: Who keeps the history of Dagbon?
According to tradition, how are Mamprugu, Dagbon, and Nanung related?
options: They were founded by sons of Naa Gbewaa and call one another brothers

activities.question: What is Naa Zanjina remembered for?
options: Moving the capital to the coast
Welcoming Islam and encouraging trade and weaving

activities.question: Apply it: Your grandmother knows the history of your family, but nothing is written down. Using the article, what is the best thing to do?
options: Listen carefully, ask questions, and write or record what she tells you
